draft.title: Index laws for algebraic products and quotients
card: To multiply terms, multiply the numbers, then add the powers of each variable. A variable with no power written has power 1.
To divide terms, divide the numbers, then subtract the powers of each variable.
Worked example: \((4a^{3}b)(2ab^{2})\). Numbers: \(4 \times 2 = 8\). Powers of \(a\): \(3 + 1 = 4\). Powers of \(b\): \(1 + 2 = 3\). The answer is \(8a^{4}b^{3}\).
Worked example: \(12x^{5} \div 3x^{2}\). Numbers: \(12 \div 3 = 4\). Powers of \(x\): \(5 - 2 = 3\). The answer is \(4x^{3}\).
draft.remember: Numbers are multiplied or divided as usual. Powers of the same variable are added to multiply and subtracted to divide.

a.why: Multiply the numbers: \(3 \times 5 = 15\). Add the powers of \(m\): \(2 + 4 = 6\). Add the powers of \(n\): \(1 + 3 = 4\). Multiplying the powers instead, as in \(m^{8}\), is a tempting mistake.
a.clue: Add powers when you multiply. Remember \(n\) has power 1.

b.why: Divide the numbers: \(20 \div 4 = 5\). Subtract the powers of \(p\): \(7 - 3 = 4\). Subtract the powers of \(q\): \(2 - 1 = 1\), so \(q\) stays. Leaving the power of \(q\) as 2, as if \(q\) had no power in the divisor, is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: A variable with no power written has power 1.

problems.detail: The why says the mistake treats q 'as if q had no power in the divisor'. The card says a variable with no power written has power 1, so this phrasing is confusing. The mistake is really ignoring q in the divisor, treating its power as 0. Reword, e.g. 'as if there were no q in the divisor'.

check.summary: Both answers are correct and the card is accurate. The only problem is that why (b) describes the mistake as treating q 'as if it had no power', which clashes with the card's rule that no power written means power 1.
